body:
Understanding the Physical States of Matter

Matter commonly exists as a solid, liquid or gas. These states differ in the arrangement, movement and interactions of their particles.

A solid ordinarily has a definite shape and volume because its particles remain in relatively fixed arrangements.

A liquid has a definite volume under ordinary conditions but takes the shape of its container because its particles can move past one another.

A gas has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume. Its particles move freely and spread to occupy the available space.

Changing the temperature or pressure can change the physical state of a substance without necessarily changing its chemical identity.

The 6 Basic Changes of State

ProcessChange of stateHeat exchange under ordinary conditions
Melting or fusionSolid to liquidHeat absorbed
Freezing or solidificationLiquid to solidHeat released
VaporisationLiquid to gasHeat absorbed
CondensationGas to liquidHeat released
SublimationSolid directly to gasHeat absorbed
DepositionGas directly to solidHeat released

In each process, the substance changes its physical state. When the change is reversible and no chemical reaction occurs, its chemical composition remains the same.

Melting and Freezing

Melting occurs when a solid changes into a liquid. For example, ice becomes liquid water when it absorbs sufficient heat.

Freezing is the reverse process. Liquid water releases heat as it changes into ice.

At normal atmospheric pressure, pure ice melts at approximately 0°C. Under the same pressure, pure water freezes at approximately 0°C.

During the melting of a pure substance at constant pressure, its temperature remains nearly constant until the phase change is completed.

The supplied energy is used to change the arrangement and interactions of particles rather than immediately increasing the temperature.

Boiling and Condensation

Boiling is a form of vaporisation in which vapour bubbles form within the liquid and rise through it.

For pure water at normal atmospheric pressure, boiling occurs at approximately 100°C.

Condensation is the reverse change from gas to liquid. When water vapour condenses, it releases energy to its surroundings.

Examples include the formation of liquid droplets on a sufficiently cold glass and the condensation of water vapour into droplets within clouds.

Why the Temperature Remains Constant During a Change of State

Consider pure ice being heated steadily at normal atmospheric pressure.

Initially, the temperature of the ice increases as it absorbs heat. When the melting point is reached, the ice begins to change into liquid water.

During melting, the temperature remains approximately 0°C until all the ice has melted, provided the pressure remains constant and the substance is pure.

After melting is complete, additional heating increases the temperature of the water until it reaches its boiling point.

During boiling, the temperature again remains nearly constant at approximately 100°C while the liquid changes into vapour.

Latent Heat

Latent heat is the energy absorbed or released during a change of physical state without a corresponding temperature change during the transition under specified conditions.

The term latent means hidden. The energy involved is not absent; it changes the physical state rather than raising or lowering the temperature during the transition.

Latent Heat of Fusion

The specific latent heat of fusion is the energy required to convert 1 kg of a solid into liquid at its melting point without changing its temperature.

The same amount of energy is released when the liquid freezes under the corresponding conditions.

Latent Heat of Vaporisation

The specific latent heat of vaporisation is the energy required to convert 1 kg of liquid into gas at its boiling point without changing its temperature.

Condensation releases the corresponding latent heat when vapour becomes liquid under the reverse conditions.

The SI unit of specific latent heat is J/kg.

Why Steam Can Cause More Severe Burns Than Boiling Water

Steam at 100°C and liquid water at 100°C have the same temperature but do not have the same internal energy per unit mass.

Steam contains additional energy associated with vaporisation.

When steam condenses on a cooler surface, it releases latent heat. This additional heat transfer can cause more severe burns than contact with the same mass of liquid water at the same initial temperature, under otherwise comparable conditions.

Sublimation and Deposition

Sublimation is the direct change of a solid into a gas without passing through the liquid state.

Examples include the conversion of dry ice, which is solid carbon dioxide, directly into carbon dioxide gas under ordinary atmospheric pressure.

Camphor and ammonium chloride are familiar school-level examples of substances that can undergo sublimation under suitable conditions.

Deposition is the reverse process in which a gas changes directly into a solid.

The formation of frost from water vapour on a sufficiently cold surface is an example of deposition.

How Pressure Affects Changes of State

The temperature at which a substance changes state depends on pressure as well as the nature of the substance.

For water, a lower external pressure generally lowers the boiling point, while a higher pressure raises it.

At high altitudes, atmospheric pressure is lower, so water boils below 100°C. In a pressure cooker, increased pressure allows water to boil at a temperature above 100°C, helping food cook more rapidly.

The familiar boiling point of 100°C is therefore not universal for water under all conditions.

Prelims focus

  • Melting and vaporisation absorb latent heat.
  • Freezing and condensation release latent heat.
  • Pure ice melts at approximately 0°C under normal atmospheric pressure.
  • Pure water boils at approximately 100°C under normal atmospheric pressure.
  • Dry ice undergoes sublimation at ordinary atmospheric pressure.
  • Trap: Continuous heating during a phase change does not necessarily produce a continuous temperature rise.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 1: Matter in Our Surroundings, sections 1.3–1.4, printed pp. 4–9, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 6: Changes Around Us, printed pp. 49–50, 2018–19 printing.]

title: Changes of State: Melting, Freezing, Boiling and Latent Heat

Why Water Can Disappear Without Boiling

Wet clothes dry even when the surrounding air is much cooler than 100°C. Similarly, water left in an open container gradually decreases in quantity without being heated to its boiling point.

These changes occur because of evaporation.

Evaporation is the change of a liquid into vapour from its exposed surface. It can occur at temperatures below the liquid's boiling point.

Liquid particles possess different amounts of kinetic energy. Some particles near the surface have sufficient energy to escape from the liquid into the gaseous state.

Because evaporation takes place at the surface, it does not require vapour bubbles to form throughout the liquid.

Evaporation Compared with Boiling

FeatureEvaporationBoiling
Where it occursAt the exposed liquid surfaceThroughout the liquid, with vapour bubbles forming
Temperature conditionCan occur below boiling temperatureOccurs at the boiling temperature for the prevailing pressure
RateMay be slow or relatively rapidRapid bulk vaporisation when sufficient heat is supplied
Effect of surface areaGreater exposed area generally increases evaporation rateBoiling behaviour depends on additional factors, including heat supply and pressure
Common exampleDrying wet clothesWater boiling in a vessel

Both processes convert liquid into gas, but their physical conditions and locations within the liquid differ.

Factors Affecting the Rate of Evaporation

Temperature

At a higher temperature, a greater fraction of liquid particles generally have enough energy to escape into the vapour state.

Consequently, evaporation usually becomes faster as temperature increases, other conditions remaining comparable.

Surface Area

When a liquid spreads over a larger exposed area, more particles can escape from its surface.

This is why spreading wet clothes helps them dry faster and why shallow water bodies can lose water rapidly through evaporation.

Humidity

Humidity describes the amount of water vapour present in the air.

When the surrounding air already contains a high proportion of water vapour relative to its capacity at that temperature, evaporation becomes slower.

Evaporation is therefore generally more effective in dry air than in highly humid air under otherwise comparable conditions.

Wind Speed

Moving air carries water vapour away from the liquid surface, reducing the accumulation of vapour immediately above it.

This generally increases evaporation.

For example, wet clothes often dry more rapidly on a warm, dry and windy day than on a humid, still day.

Why Evaporation Produces Cooling

During evaporation, particles escaping from the liquid carry energy away. The remaining liquid may therefore lose energy and become cooler.

Energy needed for continued evaporation can also be drawn from the surrounding surfaces and air.

This is the basis of evaporative cooling.

Cooling of the Human Body

The body produces sweat during hot conditions. When sweat evaporates from the skin, it removes thermal energy and helps cool the body.

Cotton clothing can absorb sweat and expose it to moving air, helping evaporation under suitable conditions.

When humidity is very high, evaporation becomes less effective, making it harder for the body to lose heat through sweating.

Cooling in an Earthen Pot

An ordinary porous earthen pot allows a small amount of water to move through its walls to the outer surface.

As this water evaporates, it absorbs energy from the pot and the water inside. Consequently, the remaining water becomes cooler.

The effect is generally stronger when the surrounding air is dry and evaporation can proceed rapidly.

Working Principle of a Desert Cooler

A desert cooler moves air through water-wetted surfaces or pads. Some water evaporates and absorbs energy from the air and wetted material, reducing the air's temperature while increasing its moisture content.

Because evaporation is less effective when the air is already humid, evaporative coolers generally work better in hot, dry climates than in highly humid climates.

Gujarat Connection: Salt Production in Kachchh

Salt production in Gujarat provides an important application of evaporation on a large scale.

The Little Rann of Kachchh is associated with traditional salt production. Saline water or brine is spread in shallow evaporation pans, where solar heating and suitable atmospheric conditions allow water to evaporate.

As water is removed, the concentration of dissolved salts increases. Under suitable conditions, salt crystallises and can be collected.

The dissolved salt does not ordinarily evaporate along with the water. The water enters the atmosphere mainly as water vapour while the dissolved salts remain behind.

This process connects the concepts of evaporation, solar heating, surface area and separation of dissolved substances.

Condensation: The Reverse of Evaporation

Condensation occurs when gas changes into liquid. Water vapour present in air can condense when it encounters sufficiently cool conditions.

For example, droplets appearing on the outside of a glass containing ice-cold water generally come from water vapour in the surrounding air.

The droplets do not normally come from water passing through the glass.

Similarly, visible mist near boiling water is composed of tiny liquid droplets formed when water vapour cools and condenses. Water vapour itself is invisible.

Condensation releases latent heat to the surroundings, whereas evaporation requires energy.

Prelims focus

  • Evaporation is a surface phenomenon; boiling is a bulk phenomenon.
  • Evaporation can occur below the boiling point.
  • Higher temperature, larger surface area and greater wind speed generally increase evaporation.
  • Higher humidity generally reduces the rate of evaporation.
  • Evaporative cooling explains sweating, earthen-pot cooling and desert coolers.
  • Trap: Water droplets on the outside of a cold glass normally form by condensation of atmospheric water vapour.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 1: Matter in Our Surroundings, section 1.5, printed pp. 9–11, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 14: Water, printed pp. 138–141, 2018–19 printing; District Kachchh, Government of Gujarat, Economy, section Salt, consulted 3 November 2026; National Remote Sensing Centre, ISRO, Salt Pan Atlas of India, Atlas Details, consulted 3 November 2026; U.S. Department of Energy, Best Management Practice 13: Other Water-Intensive Processes, section Evaporative Coolers, consulted 3 November 2026.]
